titulo: Walls of tax: the return of tariffs and what it means for open economies

fuente.nota: Escrito para el panel de idiomas. Los datos son aproximados y no deben citarse como fuente.

parrafos: For most of the past seventy years, the direction of trade policy seemed settled. Tariffs, the taxes levied on imported goods, fell steadily from the punishing levels of the interwar period to an average of only a few per cent among industrialised countries. Today that consensus has cracked. Import duties are once again being wielded as instruments of industrial policy, geopolitical leverage and domestic politics, and economies that depend heavily on trade are anxiously asking how exposed they are.

The reversal did not happen overnight. The financial crisis of 2008 dented faith in globalisation, and the rapid rise of China as a manufacturing powerhouse cost jobs in particular regions of North America and Europe, a phenomenon economists have documented in considerable detail. The political backlash took time to build, but it eventually translated into successive tariff rounds between the world’s two largest economies, which raised duties on hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of goods. Since then, protectionist measures have multiplied across the globe, and the institutions designed to restrain them have been visibly weakened.

The World Trade Organization, guardian of the multilateral rules, has been partly paralysed since its Appellate Body ceased to function in 2019 for lack of judges. Without a working court of appeal, a member that loses a dispute can simply appeal ‘into the void’, leaving the ruling in limbo indefinitely. The rules still matter, since the bulk of world trade continues to flow under them, but the threat of sanctions for breaking them has lost much of its bite. Some members have set up an interim arbitration arrangement to fill the gap, though several major economies have chosen to stay outside it.

What do tariffs actually achieve? Textbook economics offers a fairly clear answer. A duty raises the price of imported goods, which allows domestic producers to charge more and expand output, while the government collects revenue. But consumers pay higher prices and enjoy less choice, and firms that rely on imported inputs see their costs rise, which makes them less competitive abroad. In most cases the losses outweigh the gains. Studies of recent tariff rounds have found that the burden fell overwhelmingly on domestic buyers rather than on foreign exporters, contrary to the claims of their promoters.

The effects do not stop there. Tariffs tend to provoke retaliation, and the targets are often chosen for their political sensitivity: agricultural products from swing regions, emblematic brands, luxury goods. A dispute that begins over steel can quickly spread to whisky, motorcycles or olives, as Spanish farmers know only too well. Each round adds uncertainty, and uncertainty is costly in itself, because companies postpone investment until they know which markets will remain open. Some estimates suggest that trade-policy uncertainty alone has shaved several tenths of a percentage point off global growth in particularly tense years.

For small and medium-sized open economies, the stakes are especially high. A country whose exports account for a third or more of its output cannot easily replace foreign customers with domestic ones. Many European economies fall into that category, as do much of East Asia and parts of Latin America. They are also embedded in global value chains: a car assembled in Spain may contain components from a dozen countries, and a tariff imposed at any border along the way raises costs for everyone involved. In such a world, the notion that a tariff simply ‘protects’ a national industry is increasingly misleading.

Defenders of the new protectionism raise arguments that should not be dismissed out of hand. Some point to national security: the pandemic and the war in Ukraine revealed dangerous dependencies on a handful of suppliers for medicines, semiconductors and energy. Others highlight unfair competition, arguing that massive state subsidies in certain countries distort markets and that free trade only works if everyone plays by the same rules. Still others stress the social cost of deindustrialisation, which concentrated losses in communities that never shared in the gains of globalisation and whose resentment has reshaped electoral maps.

The difficulty is that tariffs are a blunt tool for addressing these concerns. Security risks can often be reduced more efficiently through stockpiles, diversification of suppliers or targeted investment. Foreign subsidies can be countered with anti-subsidy duties, which international rules allow provided they are properly investigated. And the losers from trade are better helped by retraining, regional policy and a solid safety net than by duties that raise prices for every household. Broad, across-the-board tariffs risk punishing friends and rivals alike, and they invite precisely the kind of retaliation that hurts exporters most.

The European Union finds itself in an awkward position. As the world’s largest trading bloc, with a common commercial policy managed by the Commission on behalf of all member states, it has a great deal to lose from a breakdown of the rules-based system. At the same time, it has sharpened its own defensive arsenal: an anti-coercion instrument to respond to economic blackmail, a regulation on foreign subsidies, screening of foreign investment and countervailing duties on electric vehicles imported from China. Brussels insists that these are proportionate responses consistent with WTO law; its partners do not always see it that way.

History offers a cautionary tale. In the early 1930s, a sharp rise in American tariffs triggered retaliation around the world, and the value of global trade shrank by roughly two-thirds within a few years. Most historians do not believe that tariffs caused the Great Depression, but they broadly agree that the trade war deepened and prolonged it. Countries that clung to open markets for longer found themselves with fewer and fewer customers as their neighbours retreated behind ever higher barriers. The architects of the post-war order drew a simple conclusion: rules that bind everyone are worth more than the temporary advantage any single country can extract by acting alone.

Today’s circumstances differ in important ways. Trade is far more integrated, services and data flows account for a growing share of exchanges, and supply chains are much harder to unpick. That cuts both ways: the cost of a full-blown trade war would be higher, but so is the incentive to avoid one. So far, despite the rhetoric, world trade volumes have proved surprisingly resilient, as flows have been diverted through third countries rather than halted altogether. Yet diversion is not the same as stability, and the patience of governments watching goods reroute around their barriers may prove limited.

For open economies, the sensible strategy is probably a combination of defence and diplomacy: diversifying markets through new trade agreements, strengthening tools against coercion and working with like-minded partners to repair the multilateral system rather than abandon it. For a country like Spain, which sells most of its exports to its European partners, the health of the single market is the first line of defence; but every additional market opened elsewhere is a valuable form of insurance. Tariffs may be back, but the arithmetic that made them costly has not changed. The risk is that, in trying to shield themselves from the world, countries end up building walls that mostly keep their own prosperity in.
titulo_es: Muros de impuestos: el regreso de los aranceles y lo que significa para las economías abiertas
resumen_es: Análisis del regreso del proteccionismo arancelario, sus causas, sus costes económicos y los riesgos de las guerras comerciales para economías abiertas como las europeas.

ideas_clave.idea: After decades of falling tariffs, protectionism has returned, driven by disillusion with globalisation after 2008, job losses linked to China and successive US–China tariff rounds.
The WTO has lost much of its enforcement power since its appeals body stopped working, despite an interim arbitration scheme.
According to standard economics and recent evidence, tariffs cost consumers and import-using firms more than they benefit protected producers, and the burden falls mainly on domestic buyers.
Tariffs lead to targeted retaliation and create uncertainty that delays investment and reduces global growth.
Open economies integrated into value chains, such as many in Europe, are particularly vulnerable because tariffs raise costs along the whole chain.
Supporters invoke national security, unfair subsidies and the social cost of deindustrialisation.
However, these concerns are better addressed with targeted tools such as diversification, anti-subsidy duties and support for affected workers than with broad tariffs.
The EU depends on rules-based trade but has strengthened its own defensive instruments, which partners sometimes contest.
The 1930s show how a tariff war can deepen a crisis, which inspired the post-war rules-based order.
Deeper integration makes a trade war costlier but also less likely, and trade has so far been rerouted rather than stopped.
Open economies should combine defence and diplomacy, diversifying partners and rebuilding multilateral rules, since tariffs remain economically costly.

resumen_modelo: The article analyses the comeback of tariffs and the dangers it poses for economies that depend heavily on trade. After decades of liberalisation, protectionism has gained ground since the 2008 crisis, fuelled by job losses attributed to Chinese competition and by successive tariff rounds between the United States and China, while the WTO has been weakened by the paralysis of its appeals mechanism. The author recalls that tariffs generally do more harm than good: they raise prices for consumers and costs for firms using imported inputs, and the evidence shows that domestic buyers bear most of the burden. Furthermore, they trigger retaliation aimed at politically sensitive sectors and generate uncertainty that holds back investment. Open economies embedded in global value chains, many of them European, are particularly exposed, since a duty at any border affects the whole chain. Although advocates of protection cite legitimate concerns, such as security of supply, foreign subsidies or deindustrialisation, the text argues that more targeted instruments would address them better. The EU, for its part, depends on multilateral rules yet has developed its own trade-defence tools. Drawing on the lessons of the 1930s and noting that trade has so far been diverted rather than halted, the author concludes that open economies should combine defence with diplomacy, diversifying their partners and helping to restore the multilateral system.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Average tariffs among industrialised countries rose steadily after the interwar period.
preguntas.cita: fell steadily from the punishing levels of the interwar period to an average of only a few per cent
preguntas.explicacion: Los aranceles bajaron de forma continuada desde los niveles del periodo de entreguerras hasta unos pocos puntos porcentuales; la afirmación invierte la tendencia.

preguntas.pregunta: Which of the following does the article mention as a cause of the backlash against globalisation?
opciones: Job losses in certain regions linked to China’s rise
The expansion of the European Union to the east
respuestas: Job losses in certain regions linked to China’s rise
preguntas.cita: the rapid rise of China as a manufacturing powerhouse cost jobs in particular regions of North America and Europe
preguntas.explicacion: El texto cita la crisis de 2008 y la pérdida de empleo en ciertas regiones por el ascenso industrial de China. Las demás causas no se mencionan.

preguntas.pregunta: What does it mean to appeal ‘into the void’, and why does it weaken the WTO?
respuestas: It means appealing a ruling to the Appellate Body even though it no longer works, so the dispute is never resolved. As a result, countries can break the rules without facing sanctions, and the WTO loses its enforcement power.
preguntas.cita: a member that loses a dispute can simply appeal ‘into the void’, leaving the ruling in limbo indefinitely
preguntas.explicacion: Al no haber jueces en el Órgano de Apelación, recurrir equivale a bloquear la resolución indefinidamente; las normas siguen existiendo, pero sin sanción efectiva.

preguntas.pregunta: According to studies of recent tariff rounds, who mainly bore the cost of the tariffs?
preguntas.cita: the burden fell overwhelmingly on domestic buyers rather than on foreign exporters
preguntas.explicacion: Los estudios citados concluyen que el coste recayó sobre todo en los compradores nacionales, en contra de lo que decían los promotores de los aranceles, que señalaban a los exportadores extranjeros.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 4 una palabra que signifique «represalia».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘action taken in response to an attack or harm’.
preguntas.explicacion: «Retaliation» es la represalia; en comercio, los aranceles con que un país responde a los de otro.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The text suggests that Spanish farmers have suffered from retaliatory tariffs.
preguntas.cita: A dispute that begins over steel can quickly spread to whisky, motorcycles or olives, as Spanish farmers know only too well.
preguntas.explicacion: La expresión «as Spanish farmers know only too well» indica que los agricultores españoles (aceitunas) han sufrido represalias en disputas ajenas.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Spain’s exports account for exactly a third of its output.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto habla en general de países cuyas exportaciones suponen un tercio o más del PIB y menciona un coche montado en España, pero no da el dato de las exportaciones españolas.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 6 una expresión que signifique «descartarse sin más, sin examinarse».
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning ‘rejected immediately without consideration’.
preguntas.cita: arguments that should not be dismissed out of hand
preguntas.explicacion: «To dismiss something out of hand» es rechazarlo de plano, sin pararse a considerarlo.

preguntas.pregunta: What does the author propose as a better response to foreign subsidies?
opciones: Anti-subsidy duties after a proper investigation
respuestas: Anti-subsidy duties after a proper investigation
preguntas.cita: Foreign subsidies can be countered with anti-subsidy duties, which international rules allow provided they are properly investigated.
preguntas.explicacion: El autor defiende instrumentos específicos, como los derechos antisubvención, permitidos por las normas internacionales si se investigan bien. Los aranceles generales son justo lo que critica.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The EU’s trading partners always accept that its defensive measures comply with WTO law.
preguntas.cita: Brussels insists that these are proportionate responses consistent with WTO law; its partners do not always see it that way.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que los socios de la UE no siempre lo ven así, de modo que no lo aceptan siempre.

preguntas.pregunta: What lesson did the architects of the post-war order draw from the 1930s?
respuestas: They concluded that common rules binding all countries are more valuable than the short-term gains a country can obtain by acting alone, because the tariff war of the 1930s had deepened and prolonged the Depression.
preguntas.cita: rules that bind everyone are worth more than the temporary advantage any single country can extract by acting alone
preguntas.explicacion: La respuesta debe recoger la idea de que unas reglas comunes valen más que la ventaja unilateral y relacionarla con el agravamiento de la Gran Depresión.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 10 una palabra que signifique «desviados (por otra ruta)».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘sent along a different route’.
preguntas.cita: flows have been diverted through third countries rather than halted altogether
preguntas.explicacion: «Diverted» significa desviado; en comercio internacional se habla de «trade diversion» (desviación de comercio).

preguntas.pregunta: What strategy does the author recommend for open economies?
opciones: Retaliating with higher tariffs against all partners
Combining defensive tools with diplomacy and support for multilateral rules
Focusing exclusively on the domestic market
Joining whichever bloc offers the largest market
respuestas: Combining defensive tools with diplomacy and support for multilateral rules
preguntas.cita: the sensible strategy is probably a combination of defence and diplomacy
preguntas.explicacion: El autor propone combinar defensa y diplomacia: nuevos acuerdos, instrumentos anticoerción y reparación del sistema multilateral. No defiende represalias generales ni el aislamiento.
